title: The One Where Emma Cries

jokes.text: Ross reacts to learning Rachel agreed to marry Joey: 'You said you'd marry Joey?'
jokes.setup: The audience knows the comedic bombshell — Rachel accidentally accepted Joey's proposal while exhausted after giving birth
jokes.punchline: Ross's incredulous, flat delivery of the line lands as the first big comedic reaction to this absurd situation
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom cold-open hook. Ross's disbelief is well-earned from the season 9 premiere cliffhanger. The economy of his reaction is good, but it's largely a setup for bigger laughs to follow.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I was in such an emotional state, I would have said yes to anyone who proposed to me.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I married Ross in Vegas!

jokes.text: Ross: 'I'm not helping.' — reacting to Rachel's Vegas marriage callback
jokes.setup: Rachel has just used their own marriage as proof she'd say yes to anyone
jokes.punchline: Ross's dry, defeated self-assessment: 'I'm not helping' — acknowledging his argument has collapsed
jokes.explanation: A clean button on joke #2. Ross conceding ground with resigned self-awareness is a solid character beat. Economy is near-perfect — four words do the entire job.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I married him in Vegas.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Well, Chandler's my oldest friend. Joey's my... No! Uh-uh!'
jokes.setup: Rachel deflects Ross's anger by pointing out he said Joey is his 'best friend' — implying Chandler should be
jokes.punchline: Ross starts genuinely defending the Joey/Chandler hierarchy, catches himself mid-sentence, refuses to be derailed by the technicality
jokes.explanation: Rachel's misdirection tactic almost works — the joke is that Ross's pedantic brain almost takes the bait before he course-corrects. The 'No! Uh-uh!' is a great physical/vocal button. Solid character comedy showing both Rachel's deflection instinct and Ross's susceptibility to being derailed by arguments.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, so Chandler is my best friend, but Joey is like my best friend too, just in a different way—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, wait, that's not... I'm just going to stop talking now.

jokes.text: Joey wanders into the hospital room: 'Hey, I'm gonna take off. I just wanted to say goodbye.' — sees everyone staring — 'This isn't the right room. Sorry, folks.'
jokes.setup: Tension is high in the room with Ross confronting Rachel about the proposal; Joey enters obliviously
jokes.punchline: Joey clocks the atmosphere, decides the best exit is pretending he's in the wrong room entirely and retreating
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey comedy — not dumb, but socially self-preserving. The 'wrong room' dodge is a perfect Joey solution to an uncomfortable situation. The character integration is excellent; this is exactly how Joey would handle it. Gets a big laugh on the punchline delivery and the visual of him backing out of the room.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! I'm in the wrong place!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm going to go... somewhere else. Anywhere else.

jokes.text: Phoebe shows the baby signs: 'I don't want to be negative. So I'll say most of the signs you bought are good.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been tasked with decorating with baby signs for Rachel's homecoming
jokes.punchline: Her backhanded 'most are good' implies some are very much not good, delivered with cheerful diplomacy
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's cheerful obliviousness is well-deployed. The 'I don't want to be negative, BUT...' construction is a reliable comedic frame and her earnestness makes the admission funnier. Good character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I bought an 'It's a Boy' sign, but then I found out it was a girl, so I just changed the 'B' to a 'Gr'.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'No, they ran out of "It's a Girl!" But I can fix this one.' — holds up a modified sign
jokes.setup: Phoebe admits the sign store ran out of 'It's a Girl!' signs
jokes.punchline: She has improvised a modification to an existing sign, implying a hilariously wrong or inappropriate result (inferred visual gag)
jokes.explanation: The joke lives in the visual of whatever the sign says — the transcript can't fully capture it, but Phoebe's creative problem-solving is on-brand. The 'See? Huh?' at 02:10 followed by a beat is the audience reaction to whatever abomination is on the sign. Functional Phoebe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's a Girl!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So sexy.

jokes.text: Monica looks at the modified sign Phoebe is proudly showing off: 'So sexy.' (then immediately snaps back to Chandler) 'Honey?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe shows off her badly modified sign with pride
jokes.punchline: Monica's flat 'So sexy' is her incredulous, deadpan response to what she's seeing before pivoting away — implying the sign is hilariously inappropriate
jokes.explanation: Two words doing heavy lifting. Monica's withering sarcasm on the sign, then immediately pivoting to find her husband, is a quick efficient joke. Timing-dependent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross and Rachel will be back soon.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Great! Because I've decided they're being moved to Thursday nights at 8.

jokes.text: Chandler's sleep-deprivation spiral: 'I started worrying about this big divisional meeting I have today. The more I worried, the more I couldn't sleep. If I fall asleep now I'll get six hours. If I fall asleep now I'll get five hours...'
jokes.setup: Chandler explains why he's exhausted — he had a big meeting and couldn't sleep
jokes.punchline: He describes the universal anxiety of watching the clock while trying to sleep, counting down hours with increasing desperation
jokes.explanation: Highly relatable observational joke that lands well with audiences. The escalating countdown is a solid comedic structure. Not particularly original but executed with good specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I calculated that if I go to sleep right now, I can get four hours of sleep before I have to wake up.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, that would've put me right to sleep.

jokes.text: Monica: 'You know what you should've done? Told yourself that little story.' — after Chandler describes his insomnia spiral
jokes.setup: Chandler has just finished describing a torturous night of clock-watching anxiety
jokes.punchline: Monica suggests he should have used his own boring story as a sleep aid — undercutting the relatability of his complaint
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-structured comeback. Monica's sharpness is perfectly in character. The joke reframes his complaint as the cure — good logical inversion. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, this is... this is huge. How am I supposed to... I mean, where would I even... Oh! It's so... cute! Thank you so much!

jokes.text: Rachel sees the giant stuffed gorilla: 'Oh, my gosh. Look, there's something every mother needs. A giant, stuffed gorilla that takes up the entire apartment.'
jokes.setup: Rachel comes home and sees the pile of gifts, then spots the enormous gorilla
jokes.punchline: Her mock-enthusiastic 'every mother needs' framing before landing on the absurd item — then immediately pivoting to 'Oh, you guys, I love it'
jokes.explanation: The visual of the apartment-dominating gorilla is the real joke. Rachel's framing adds to it. The quick pivot to genuine affection ('Oh, I love it') is a nice character beat showing new-mom warmth cutting through her usual sarcasm.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what I want? I want a teepee.

jokes.text: Joey: 'I didn't think I should be here either. But somebody said he'd be over it.' / 'Hey, what do I know? I wanted to get a bigger gorilla.'
jokes.setup: Monica scolds Joey for being there when Ross arrives, since he's still mad
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he correctly assessed the situation but was overruled — then undercuts any claim to wisdom by revealing his only opinion was about gorilla size
jokes.explanation: Two-beat Joey joke that works well. First beat: he had social awareness (surprising). Second beat: the only thing he contributed to the planning was wanting a BIGGER gorilla (perfectly Joey). The escalation from 'I knew better' to 'I wanted an even bigger gorilla' is a great character-specific comedic reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, she's so cute, I could just eat her up!

jokes.text: Chandler's divisional meeting: presenter drones through city-by-city failures — 'Boston is down. Atlanta is down. Houston is down. I could go on and on. But instead of boring you... I'll go straight to my 42-point plan.'
jokes.setup: We cut to Chandler in a corporate meeting, clearly sleep-deprived. The presenter lists failing offices
jokes.punchline: The presenter's offer to spare them from boredom leads directly to announcing a 42-point plan — which is obviously MORE boring
jokes.explanation: Good comic absurdism in the corporate setting. The presenter's oblivious self-contradiction (not boring you → 42-point plan) is well-constructed. This also sets up Chandler falling asleep, earning the later payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I know! I'd start with the soft parts—the ears and the little baby toes. Maybe work my way up to the sweet, sweet thighs. And then I'd save the head for last because that's where all the delicious brains are!

jokes.text: Phoebe, looking at baby Emma: 'Oh, I just want to bite her ear off and use it as a sucking candy.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is cooing over newborn Emma, expressing how cute she is
jokes.punchline: Her expression of affection escalates into a surreally violent image — biting the ear off and using it as candy — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe escalation joke. The 'I want to eat the cute baby' trope exists, but the specific detail of 'use it as a sucking candy' pushes it into genuinely dark-absurdist territory that's distinctively Phoebe. The character integration is excellent — only Phoebe can say this and have it read as pure sweetness. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You guys own a hospital?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, I left them at the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you just abandoned your diapers at the hospital? That's so irresponsible!

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'But I could take one of those little feet and put it in a pita pocket.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe already described wanting to eat Emma's ear; she continues with another body part
jokes.punchline: The pita pocket specification — a food detail so mundane and domestic it makes the cannibalistic image even more absurd
jokes.explanation: The escalation from ear-candy to foot-in-pita-pocket is comedy gold. The pita pocket is the key detail — it's so specific and mundane that it makes the whole thing land harder. This is the funnier of the two baby-eating jokes because the mundane food specificity elevates the absurdity. Highly quotable, distinctly Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, take your time. It's not like you made any hasty decisions lately.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I mean, what's the worst that could happen? You end up with a blueberry instead of chocolate chip?

jokes.text: Ross's diaper reveal: Rachel asks where the diapers are. Ross: 'In the hospital.' — pause — 'I, uh, left the diapers at the hospital.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is efficiently debriefing Ross on where everything was put away
jokes.punchline: Ross says 'In the hospital' as if it's a flex — then has to clarify he means he forgot them there
jokes.explanation: Good two-beat structure. 'In the hospital' reads as a confident answer before collapsing into admission of error. The beat between the lines is where the joke lives — the audience registers the error a half-second before Ross clarifies.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How long do you think he'll stay mad?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, I don't know. How long were we broken up for?

jokes.text: Joey: 'Wow, you guys got a hospital? Fancy.'
jokes.setup: Ross says the diapers are 'in the hospital'
jokes.punchline: Joey mishears/misunderstands it as Rachel and Ross having their own personal hospital — and is impressed
jokes.explanation: Very economical Joey joke. 'Fancy' is the perfect word choice — it communicates his genuine impressed-ness in one syllable. The misunderstanding is classic Joey but not in a lazy way; his brain goes to 'personal hospital' because that tracks with his logic. High character integration, excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: When do you think Emma will wake up?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, probably around noon. She likes to sleep in. We have an arrangement — I don't bother her before 10, and she doesn't bother me before 10.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Please, take your time. It's an important decision, not like... say, I don't know, deciding to marry someone. This is about a muffin.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has been taking an extremely long time deciding what kind of muffin she wants while Ross is waiting
jokes.punchline: Ross cannot help himself — the muffin-ordering becomes a vehicle for his real grievance about the marriage proposal
jokes.explanation: Ross's inability to let go of his grievance, even during a mundane muffin order, is pitch-perfect character comedy. The structure — building up 'important decision' before revealing it's about the marriage, then puncturing it with 'this is about a muffin' — is well-crafted. His barely-contained sarcasm is a great Ross mode and the line is quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Don't wake the baby!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's okay, I'm the mother. I made her.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'I don't know. He got over the "We were on a break" thing quickly.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel speculate how long Ross will stay angry about the Joey proposal
jokes.punchline: Rachel references the most famous and prolonged grudge in Ross's history — 'we were on a break' — as the benchmark for 'getting over things quickly'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The callback to 'we were on a break' — arguably the most famous running joke in Friends history — is deployed with perfect irony. Rachel using it as her example of Ross 'getting over things quickly' is a devastating piece of character comedy. The audience recognition is instant and the laugh is huge. Economy is superb — the whole joke lives in the callback being treated as evidence of rapid emotional healing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, there's your 'I told you so'

jokes.text: Rachel decides to wake the sleeping baby: 'Well, I can do whatever I want. I made her.'
jokes.setup: Monica warns Rachel you should never wake a sleeping baby
jokes.punchline: Rachel's ownership logic — 'I made her' — as justification for violating basic baby wisdom
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical Rachel line. The 'I made her' ownership logic is fundamentally absurd but delivered with Rachel's total confidence. It's also a good setup for the immediate consequence — the baby screams. The punchline is both the line AND what follows.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So when can we give it back?

jokes.text: Emma immediately starts screaming after Rachel wakes her. Monica: 'Well, I would say I told you so, but she's kind of doing that for me.'
jokes.setup: Monica warned Rachel not to wake the baby; Rachel did it anyway; baby immediately screams
jokes.punchline: Monica's dry observation that the screaming baby is her 'I told you so'
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-timed payoff to the previous beat. The structure is tight: setup (don't wake baby), transgression (Rachel wakes baby), consequence (screaming), and Monica's reaction delegating the 'I told you so' to the baby. Gets a solid laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: You're going to love Tulsa! It's got everything — a river, a couple of chains restaurants, and some really great dust storms.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, what's not to love?

jokes.text: Joey, as Emma screams: 'How long do you think we have to stay?'
jokes.setup: Everyone is reacting to the heartbreaking sound of the screaming newborn with sympathy
jokes.punchline: Joey cuts through the sentiment with pure self-interest — his only concern is his own exit strategy
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey economy. While everyone else is emotionally invested, Joey is pragmatically wondering when he can leave. The timing against the screaming baby makes it land harder. Character integration is excellent — this is quintessential Joey selfishness played as innocence.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The book says here that you shouldn't wake the baby.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, maybe if you had a time machine, you could go back and not wake the baby in the first place!

jokes.text: Chandler, in the meeting: Boss asks 'Are you on board?' Chandler: 'Yes.' Boss: 'Well, then problem solved. Chandler will run our office in Tulsa. You're gonna love Oklahoma.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is visibly falling asleep in the meeting; everyone else has agreed to something
jokes.punchline: His sleep-addled 'Yes' to 'are you on board' is interpreted as volunteering to move to Tulsa and run the Oklahoma office
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom premise delivered cleanly. The structure is excellent — the sleep deprivation from the opening pays off here as the comedic consequence. The 'You're gonna love Oklahoma' kicker lands perfectly. This sets up an entire B-plot, so it earns high marks for both the joke and its structural function.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It worked! The rapid swinging stopped the baby from crying!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, the baby didn't stop crying because of the swinging. The baby paused to vomit from motion sickness.

jokes.text: Phoebe, while trying to calm Emma: 'Oh, try this one. "Go back in time and listen to Phoebe."'
jokes.setup: Everyone is scrambling to find solutions for the crying baby; someone suggests something from a book
jokes.punchline: Phoebe suggests the technique of time travel to prevent Rachel from waking the baby — presented as genuine parenting advice
jokes.explanation: Sharp callback that also works as pure Phoebe character comedy. The specificity of 'go back in time and listen to Phoebe' — presented as a baby-calming technique from a book — is both a good I-told-you-so jab and a funny absurdist frame. The 'I told you so' energy through a sci-fi lens is distinctly Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, it's crying again.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It? It's a baby, Rachel. A baby is a 'he' or a 'she,' not an 'it.'

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I don't know if it's a boy or a girl!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Then ask! Don't just refer to a human being as 'it.'

jokes.text: Ross reads: 'It says to try holding the baby close to your body and then swing her rapidly from side to side.' — everyone tries it — silence — 'It worked!' — then Monica immediately stops to throw up
jokes.setup: Ross reads a baby-calming technique from a book; they try rapid side-to-side swinging
jokes.punchline: Brief apparent success ('it worked!') immediately undercut by Monica stopping to vomit from dizziness
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy beat. The fake-out success ('it worked!') followed immediately by the adult getting dizzy and nauseated is a well-structured reversal. The baby is fine; the adult is the casualty. The visual of Monica stopping to vomit while the baby just stares is funny on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can't believe this baby won't stop crying! Ross, this is all your fault!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: My fault? How is this my fault?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, if you were a better... you know... we wouldn't have had this baby in the first place!

jokes.text: Monica: 'She, Rach. Not it. She.' Rachel: 'Yeah. I'm not so sure.'
jokes.setup: Rachel, exhausted and losing her mind, refers to her own baby as 'it' — Monica corrects her
jokes.punchline: Rachel's doubtful 'I'm not so sure' — she's not even confident her child is human at this point
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy about new parenthood. Rachel's total dissociation from her baby's humanity after hours of screaming is a real and funny emotion played perfectly. The 'I'm not so sure' is a great punchline — it's both funny and an honest representation of new-parent exhaustion. Character-specific to new-mom Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: A baby? Ross and Rachel are having a baby? Well, I hope the kid has Rachel's looks and Ross's... well, actually, I hope it just has Rachel's looks. Poor kid doesn't stand a chance with those Geller genes.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'All right, this just proves no good can come from having sex with Ross!'
jokes.setup: Rachel is at her wit's end with the screaming baby, connecting cause and effect
jokes.punchline: She traces her suffering back to its source — sex with Ross — as the original sin leading to this screaming nightmare
jokes.explanation: Good laugh line. The logical chain from screaming baby → sex with Ross is funny and character-appropriate. It also adds a layer by being the kind of thing Rachel would say — blaming Ross for consequences of a decision she participated in. Decent quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: She'll never be with you. She doesn't even know you exist.

jokes.text: Gunther: 'I can't even believe she slept with you in the first place.' — to Ross about Rachel
jokes.setup: Gunther is filling Ross's diaper errand order; they're discussing Rachel having his baby
jokes.punchline: Gunther's long-running obsession with Rachel manifests as genuine incredulity that she'd sleep with Ross
jokes.explanation: Classic Gunther joke relying entirely on his well-established Rachel obsession. The character integration is excellent — only Gunther would express his love by insulting Ross's attractiveness to Rachel. Functional but not novel; it's a familiar Gunther beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, what are you doing with your hands?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: They're air quotes.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh. I thought you were trying to catch something invisible.

jokes.text: Ross's confused 'Huh?' reaction to Gunther — followed by Gunther's flustered cover attempt — followed by another 'Huh?'
jokes.setup: Gunther has just said he can't believe Rachel slept with Ross; Ross is trying to process this
jokes.punchline: The extended awkward exchange of Gunther trying to walk it back while Ross stares blankly — the discomfort IS the joke
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'Huh?' with the timestamp gap suggests extended comedic business between Gunther and Ross that the transcript can't fully capture — visual awkwardness, Gunther's flailing attempt to explain. Functional cringe-adjacent comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So you just do this? *makes air quotes gesture incorrectly*

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, no! Joey, that's not how you do air quotes.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'm doing it exactly like you showed me!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You have to use two fingers on each hand, and you actually have to make the quote mark motion.

jokes.text: Joey defends himself: 'Let's put aside the fact that you "accidentally" picked up my grandmother's ring and you "accidentally" proposed to Rachel.' Joey air-quotes 'accidentally'
jokes.setup: Ross is confronting Joey about the accidental proposal
jokes.punchline: Ross uses air quotes sarcastically around 'accidentally' to imply Joey was deliberate — setting up Joey's response about not knowing what air quotes mean
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the air-quotes punchline that follows. Gets moderate laugh on the sarcasm but the real payoff is the next beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, you know what? Fine! I'll hit you!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah? Come on!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: *swings*

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: *ducks* Whoa, whoa, whoa!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What are you doing?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'm sorry, it's instinct!

jokes.text: Joey: 'Can I just stop you there for a second? When people do this: [air quotes] I don't really know what that means.'
jokes.setup: Ross uses aggressive air quotes while confronting Joey
jokes.punchline: Joey genuinely doesn't understand the gesture and admits it — derailing Ross's righteous anger with pure obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Very well-executed Joey joke. The comedic mechanism — Joey's obliviousness completely defusing Ross's anger by forcing a detour into gesture explanation — is structurally elegant. It's not a dumb joke about Joey being stupid; it's a joke about how his lack of cultural knowledge has a physics-defying ability to derail any confrontation. Character integration is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You gotta do it like this.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Duck!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Duck!

jokes.text: Joey: 'I know. I should've. "I'm sorry."' — with air quotes around 'I'm sorry' — Ross: 'Not using it right, Joe.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just had the air-quotes concept explained to him; he immediately tries to use them
jokes.punchline: He misapplies them to 'I'm sorry' — suggesting his apology is insincere (or meaningless) — Ross has to point out the error
jokes.explanation: This is the best payoff in the Joey/Ross confrontation sequence. The escalation from 'I don't understand air quotes' to 'I'll try air quotes' to accidentally using them to imply his apology is sarcastic is brilliantly structured. Ross's flat 'Not using it right, Joe' is the perfect button. The layering — Joey trying to learn, immediately misapplying, inadvertently sabotaging his own apology — is excellent sitcom craft. This gets an 8 because it's genuinely impressive joke construction.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Maybe she saw The Notebook.

jokes.text: Joey, after Ross corrects him: '[corrected air quotes] "I'm sorry."' — still using air quotes on his second attempt
jokes.setup: Ross has told Joey he's not using air quotes right; Joey tries again
jokes.punchline: He still uses air quotes on the apology — either not understanding the correction or choosing the wrong word to quote
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the running gag — Joey's second attempt still fails, suggesting he either can't or won't stop using quotes on 'sorry.' The persistence of the error after correction is funnier than the first misuse.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, so that's what I've been missing! I could've married Chandler and been part of all the husband-and-wife stuff!

jokes.text: Joey: 'Now you should scream at me or curse me or hit me. / You'll feel better. I'll feel better.'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to resolve the tension with Ross, who won't engage
jokes.punchline: Joey's solution — physical violence as emotional resolution — presented as mutually beneficial therapy
jokes.explanation: Joey's fight-as-therapy logic is funny and character-specific. The 'I'll feel better' addition is key — his masochism is presented as generosity. Sets up the physical comedy that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. Tulsa is just like New York... if New York were flat, had no Broadway, and everyone there drove pickup trucks.

jokes.text: Joey goads Ross into swinging at him — 'A little bit. Little bit. A little bit more.' — escalating until Ross finally swings — Joey ducks — Ross punches the hospital sign
jokes.setup: Joey has convinced Ross to hit him to release his anger; the tension escalates through Joey's taunting countdown
jokes.punchline: Joey's reflex duck means Ross punches the wall/sign instead, hurting himself — the aggressor becomes the victim
jokes.explanation: Excellent physical comedy sequence with a well-structured escalation. The repeated 'little bit' taunt building to the swing — then Joey's survival instinct betraying him by ducking — is a perfect physical comedy inversion. Ross ends up injured despite being the 'victim' of the original transgression. The escalation structure (no, no, no → full swing) is well-paced and the punchline lands hard on physical comedy grounds.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, Monica, let me get this straight. You're comparing Tulsa to Paris? That's like comparing a gas station bathroom to the Louvre. One has a toilet that probably works half the time, and the other is in France.

jokes.text: Joey: 'You were supposed to duck! Why didn't you?' Ross: 'Let's talk on the way to the hospital.' Joey: 'Good. Yeah, maybe while we're there, they can check your reflexes.'
jokes.setup: Ross has just punched a sign and broken his thumb; Joey is explaining the duck was a reflex
jokes.punchline: Joey suggests checking Ross's reflexes at the hospital — obliviously pointing out that Ross's failure to duck caused his injury, essentially blaming the victim with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Joey's reflexes-check suggestion is a perfect button on the physical comedy sequence. His logic is internally consistent — if Ross had ducked, he wouldn't have broken his thumb — which makes him completely immune to any culpability in his mind. The character voice is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, are you telling me you're moving to Oklahoma, or are you coming out?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm trying to cheer you up!

jokes.text: Joey, explaining the reflex: 'When a fist comes at your face, you duck.' — then demonstrates by literally ducking — 'Look.'
jokes.setup: Ross is furious that Joey ducked; Joey defends himself
jokes.punchline: Joey demonstrates ducking mid-argument as if this is news to Ross — his earnest explanation of a thing everyone knows, delivered as revelation
jokes.explanation: Joey's sincerity in explaining ducking — as if Ross doesn't understand reflexes — is very Joey. The physical demonstration ('Look') mid-explanation is the visual punch. His earnestness is the core of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: They offered me a pathetically modest car lease as my only compensation.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'You guys, we can't turn on each other, okay? That's just what she wants.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel are snapping at each other while trying to calm the screaming baby
jokes.punchline: Phoebe attributes strategy and malevolent intent to the newborn — as if the baby is deliberately running a divide-and-conquer operation
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. Phoebe treating the newborn as a calculating tactical adversary — 'that's just what she wants' — is a perfect absurdist concept delivered with complete sincerity. It's distinctly Phoebe (she'd genuinely believe this), well-structured, economical, highly quotable, and gets a big laugh. The logic is both insane and weirdly applicable to any group being stressed by a common problem.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What's wrong with Emma? Why is she crying?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: She overheard us talking about Tulsa.

jokes.text: Phoebe, excluded from the husband-wife conversation: 'I knew I should've married Chandler.'
jokes.setup: Monica tells Phoebe the conversation is a 'husband-and-wife kind of thing' and Phoebe can't join
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's instant regret that she didn't marry Chandler — so she could be included in the conversation — presented as a purely practical calculation
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical Phoebe line. The implication — that she'd marry Chandler purely for the administrative access — is both funny and very Phoebe. No sentiment, just practical access calculation. Good character voice and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not sleeping, I'm just resting my eyes. It's like meditation, but with more drool.

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: That's not funny, Bing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I can see that by the complete lack of laughter in the room. It's like a silent film, except without the artistic merit.

jokes.text: Chandler sets up moving to Paris: 'You know how people say that Tulsa... is the Paris of Oklahoma?'
jokes.setup: Chandler is building toward revealing they have to move to Tulsa; he frames it with the 'Paris of Oklahoma' construction
jokes.punchline: The sheer audacity of invoking Paris to sell Tulsa — and Monica's absolutely withering response
jokes.explanation: Classic build-up joke. The '...is the Paris of Oklahoma?' delivery — with the pause — is structurally excellent. The audience gets ahead of Chandler and laughs before Monica can respond. The long setup ('we said Paris... French cooking... picnics along the Seine') makes the Tulsa reveal land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Sir, I really don't want to go to Tulsa. It's a terrible place. Nothing good ever happens in Tulsa.

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? Tulsa is wonderful! It's got great restaurants, beautiful parks...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, but—

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: And the people there are incredibly friendly. World-class museums. A thriving arts scene.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I understand, but I really can't—

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: The sunsets are breathtaking. It's practically the Paris of Oklahoma.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Please, I—

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: I'm thinking of moving there myself. It's basically a utopia. Shangri-La. The Garden of Eden before the fall.

jokes.text: Monica: 'What? Who says that? People who have never been to Paris?'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just said 'people say Tulsa is the Paris of Oklahoma'
jokes.punchline: Monica's two-step: incredulity ('who says that?') immediately answered by herself ('people who've never been to Paris')
jokes.explanation: Monica answering her own rhetorical question is a satisfying comedic structure. 'People who have never been to Paris' is a great punchline — it both destroys the comparison and implies that everyone saying it is provincial. Good economy, strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Can I call you Carol?

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: My name is Carol.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, thank God. I had no idea what your name was.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Tulsa, Oklahoma?' / 'The Sooner State.' / 'Whatever that is.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks for confirmation they're moving to Tulsa, Oklahoma
jokes.punchline: Chandler offers the state nickname — 'The Sooner State' — as if it helps, then immediately admits he doesn't know what that means
jokes.explanation: Good self-undermining joke. Chandler tries to seem informed, immediately reveals he isn't. 'Whatever that is' is the honest button that makes it work. Functional comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, she has very strong, masculine features. Very angular. She could be a, uh, diesel mechanic or a lumberjack.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Chandler, I don't even want to see the musical Oklahoma. "Oh, What a Beautiful Mornin'"? "Surrey With the Fringe on Top"? Are you trying to tell me we're moving to Oklahoma or that you're gay?'
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to sell Monica on Tulsa/Oklahoma and starts quoting the musical Oklahoma
jokes.punchline: Monica interprets his song knowledge as a potential coming-out moment — the Oklahoma songs acting as evidence of hidden sexuality
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the recurring Friends meta-joke about Chandler's sexuality being ambiguous. The specific song title citations ('Surrey with the Fringe on Top') ground it. Monica's deadpan delivery of 'are you gay?' lands as a solid punchline. Gets a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can help you fill out those forms with your broken thumb.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh sure, because that's exactly what I need right now - someone touching my injury while I'm vulnerable and in pain.

jokes.text: Monica: 'All right, not that this matters, but did they at least offer you a huge raise?' Chandler: 'No. But they are going to lease us a Ford Focus.'
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to find ANY silver lining in the Tulsa move
jokes.punchline: The compensation package is a leased Ford Focus — the most underwhelming possible car to anchor a major life upheaval
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic anticlimax. After the huge setup of uprooting their lives for Tulsa, the compensation is a leased Ford Focus. The specificity of 'Ford Focus' (not 'a nice car,' not even 'a car' — a Ford Focus) is what makes it land. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What is Ross short for?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, I mean what's it short for? Like how Bob is short for Robert.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh. Um, it's just Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, what about... Roseph? Or Rosario?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, it's just Ross.

jokes.text: Monica: 'What is wrong with Emma?' Phoebe: 'Oh, she misunderstood. She thought she was moving to Tulsa.'
jokes.setup: Emma is screaming; Monica asks what's wrong; Phoebe provides an explanation
jokes.punchline: Phoebe attributes the baby's crying to having overheard the Tulsa discussion and being upset about it — treating the newborn as a fully comprehending party
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Phoebe synthesizes both the A and B plots by giving the screaming baby a rational motivation — she overheard the Tulsa discussion. The delivery is classic Phoebe: treating a newborn as a sentient, geographically opinionated person. The callback structure (Tulsa + crying baby) gives it extra comedic weight. Excellent character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: When's Ross's birthday again?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: May.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Right, right, May... or was it September?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's May, Joe.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, yeah, May-tember. I got it now.

jokes.text: Chandler tells his boss he can't move: 'It's a funny story, actually. Ha ha. I kind of fell asleep in the meeting this morning. So when I said I'd move to Tulsa, I didn't really know what I was saying.'
jokes.setup: Chandler goes to his boss to get out of the Tulsa assignment
jokes.punchline: His explanation — 'I was asleep' — delivered with 'it's a funny story' framing to a clearly unamused boss
jokes.explanation: Cringe comedy as Chandler tries to sell his terrible excuse. The 'ha ha' laugh he inserts himself is a great Chandler nervous-tic. The boss's silence and 'you fell asleep?' is the deadpan response that makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. I'm not a dinosaur. I'm a paleontologist. A paleontologist studies dinosaurs. There's a big difference.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, to me, you're a dinosaur.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm a... you know what? Never mind.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Isn't that funny? / Irony. Not a fan? All right.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has explained to his boss that he was up all night worrying about the meeting — and therefore fell asleep during it
jokes.punchline: He points out the irony himself, gets no reaction, and retreats — 'Irony. Not a fan? All right.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chandler cringe comedy. His compulsion to explain the irony of his situation to a boss who is clearly not finding it funny, then noticing the non-reaction and folding — 'Not a fan? All right.' — is a perfect character beat. The economy is great and it's very quotable. This is Chandler at his most Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's why it's so important to stick to your plans. You can't just abandon your commitments because something else comes along. It's about discipline and—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hold on, my phone's ringing.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'See me, I love Tulsa. Tulsa is heaven. Tulsa is Italy. Please don't make me go there.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is desperately trying to appeal to his boss while simultaneously needing to get out of the move
jokes.punchline: His overcorrecting enthusiasm ('Tulsa is Italy!') immediately followed by begging not to be sent there — the two positions coexisting in one breath
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler panic escalation — his praise of Tulsa goes hyperbolic as his desperation rises, then collapses into the admission. 'Tulsa is Italy' is a good absurdist escalation before the deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what they say - misery loves company.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, misery just moved in with us.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Look, Carol. Can I call you Carol?' Boss: '...Why would I when your name is Elaine?'
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to build false rapport with his boss by using a name
jokes.punchline: He's gotten her name completely wrong — she's Elaine, not Carol
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat. The 'can I call you Carol' formula backfires because that's not her name. The boss's dry correction ('why would I when your name is Elaine?') lands well. Chandler's hole keeps getting deeper.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, I figured out the whole work thing, so how hard can mothering be?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, you can't just use your sex appeal on a baby.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'What a great picture of your son. Strapping.' Boss: stare. Chandler: 'That's a picture of your daughter, isn't it?'
jokes.setup: Chandler is desperately trying to build rapport after getting her name wrong
jokes.punchline: He compliments her 'son' — it's her daughter — and then completes the humiliation by adding 'she's lovely, I like a girl with a strong jaw'
jokes.explanation: Each new Chandler gaffe compounds the previous one. The 'strong jaw' cover saves it from being a standard misread-the-picture joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Monica. With skills like that, no wonder Chandler's always so happy.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Well, she's lovely. I like a girl with a strong jaw.' — then: 'I'll call you from Tulsa.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just called the boss's daughter a boy and is trying to recover
jokes.punchline: 'I like a girl with a strong jaw' — an insult disguised as a compliment — followed by complete resignation: 'I'll call you from Tulsa'
jokes.explanation: One of the best Chandler moments in the episode. 'I like a girl with a strong jaw' is a genuinely funny line — a compliment so backhanded it's weaponized — delivered as his attempt to salvage the situation. Then the immediate full capitulation — 'I'll call you from Tulsa' — is the perfect button. The transition from 'I'll fight this' to total defeat in one breath, with 'strong jaw' as the moment of surrender, is excellent comedic structure. This is Chandler at his most self-defeating and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh thank god, the baby's finally quiet.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can actually hear myself think again. Although, to be honest, all I hear are voices telling me I'm doing everything wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm kidding! I'm kidding. Those are just my mother.

jokes.text: Joey: 'That's weird. Are you sure you're punching right? Make a fist.'
jokes.setup: Joey learns Ross broke his thumb from the punch — which was meant to hit Joey
jokes.punchline: Joey questions Ross's punching technique — implying the problem was Ross's form, not the fact that Joey ducked
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey response to Ross's injury. His instinct is to give Ross punching lessons while Ross holds a broken hand. The character logic is impeccable — Joey takes zero responsibility and pivots to coaching. 'Make a fist' while Ross has a broken thumb is a great visual comedy detail.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, you can never leave this apartment. Your baby-calming skills are too valuable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? Rachel, I have a life!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Not anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, how about I'm here Monday through Thursday, and weekends I'm free?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Deal.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Why, does it look like I'm having trouble with my misshapen claw?'
jokes.setup: Joey offers to help Ross fill out the hospital forms with his broken thumb
jokes.punchline: Ross describes his broken-thumb hand as a 'misshapen claw' — both graphic and self-pitying in a very Ross way
jokes.explanation: 'Misshapen claw' is a genuinely funny, specific piece of language. Ross's flair for melodramatic self-description is a good character trait deployed well here. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're moving to Tulsa.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Shh!

jokes.text: Joey fills out forms: 'No, I know Ross. But what's it short for? Like Rossell. Or... Rosstrophor.'
jokes.setup: Joey is filling out hospital forms for Ross; asks Ross's name
jokes.punchline: Joey hypothesizes that 'Ross' is short for something — specifically 'Rossell' or 'Rosstrophor' — two completely invented names
jokes.explanation: 'Rosstrophor' is the standout word in the episode. Joey's completely sincere invention of elongated versions of a simple name — including one that sounds like a pharmaceutical — is excellent absurdist character comedy. The specificity of 'Rosstrophor' elevates this above generic Joey confusion. High quotability, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What happened to your hand?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, I broke it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God! How?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, you should see the other guy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey!

jokes.text: Joey, after Ross confirms just 'Ross': 'Oh. It's pretty.'
jokes.setup: Joey was clearly hoping 'Ross' was short for something more elaborate
jokes.punchline: His slight disappointment followed by genuine appreciation of the simplicity: 'Oh. It's pretty.'
jokes.explanation: Beautiful button on the name sequence. Joey's earnest 'It's pretty' — applied to the mundane name 'Ross' that he's known for years — is a perfect Joey non-sequitur delivered with complete sincerity. Economy is near-perfect (three words) and it gets a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: This is hard.

jokes.text: Joey: 'May... tember?' — guessing Ross's birthday month
jokes.setup: Joey claims to know Ross's birthday while filling out the form
jokes.punchline: His confident 'Sure.' collapses into the completely invented month of 'May-tember' — a hybrid that doesn't exist
jokes.explanation: 'Maytember' is a classic Joey word-invention. The structure is perfect — the confident 'Sure' selling us on his knowledge, then the portmanteau of two months into a non-existent hybrid delivered with the same confidence — is excellent. Very quotable, excellent economy, and deeply character-specific. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's a natural instinct!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: *makes threatening gesture at Ross*

jokes.text: Joey, for 'Occupation': 'Dinosaurs.' — Ross: 'Actually, I'm a paleon—' — 'Dinosaurs is fine.'
jokes.setup: Joey is writing Ross's occupation on the hospital form
jokes.punchline: Ross starts to correct 'Dinosaurs' to 'paleontologist' but then immediately accepts 'Dinosaurs' — suggesting it's close enough and he has no energy left
jokes.explanation: Very strong joke. Joey reduces Ross's academic career to 'Dinosaurs,' which is both reductive and weirdly accurate. Ross's 'Actually I'm a paleon—... Dinosaurs is fine' is the killer line — his defeated acceptance is funnier than any correction would be. Extremely economical. This is one of the most rewatchable moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Occupation? Dinosaurs.' Ross: 'Actually, I'm a paleon—' Joey: 'Dinosaurs is fine.'
jokes.setup: Joey is filling out 'occupation' on the hospital form
jokes.punchline: Joey writes 'Dinosaurs,' Ross starts to correct him with 'paleon[tologist],' and Joey cuts him off — 'Dinosaurs is fine' — shutting down the correction with editorial authority
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Dinosaurs is fine' — Joey's authoritative dismissal of Ross's professional credential in favor of his own simplified version — is delivered with complete confidence. The structure is perfect: Ross starts the correction, Joey cuts him off as if he's the expert here. The economy is exceptional. It's a joke that also inadvertently captures how many people actually think of Ross's job. Very quotable, strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: 'The drawing is not.' — Joey apparently drew a dinosaur next to 'Dinosaurs' on the form; Ross's reaction to it
jokes.setup: Joey has written 'Dinosaurs' as Ross's occupation — implying he also illustrated it
jokes.punchline: Ross's flat 'The drawing is not [fine]' — confirming Joey has drawn a dinosaur on the official hospital form
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the hospital form sequence. The implication that Joey drew a dinosaur next to 'Dinosaurs' on a medical form — and Ross's resigned acknowledgment — is a great visual gag that the audience has to construct from the dialogue. Economy is exceptional. Extends the previous joke elegantly.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Relationship?' (to Ross about Rachel as emergency contact) — Ross's long pause — Joey: 'You guys are more than that. You're gonna get together, right?'
jokes.setup: Joey asks what Ross's relationship is to emergency contact Rachel
jokes.punchline: Joey pushes back on Ross's reluctance to define the relationship — revealing Joey genuinely ships them — while also functioning as an ironic beat given the episode's tension
jokes.explanation: More of a character/emotional beat than a pure joke, but the irony of Joey — who accidentally proposed to Rachel — being the one pushing Ross to pursue her adds comedic texture. Gets a mild laugh from the irony.

jokes.text: Ross: 'I don't want to be just anybody.' — reacting to Joey pointing out Rachel would have said yes to anyone
jokes.setup: Joey is explaining that Rachel's acceptance was meaningless — she was exhausted, she'd have said yes to anyone
jokes.punchline: Ross's quiet 'I don't want to be just anybody' — both genuinely heartfelt AND accidentally funny given the context (Joey is literally 'anybody' in this scenario)
jokes.explanation: Straddles comedy and genuine emotion — which is a Friends specialty. The line works as Ross pathos but also gets a smile because 'anybody' was Joey, and Joey is very literally 'anybody' in this context. Good economy.

jokes.text: Ross: 'And if you have a plan, you should stick to it. That's why they call them plans. Hello? Ha ha.'
jokes.setup: Ross is convincing himself (and Joey) that he's fine with just being Emma's co-parent — no romantic feelings
jokes.punchline: His circular tautology ('that's why they call them plans') and self-conscious laugh betraying his lack of conviction
jokes.explanation: Ross's tautological self-reassurance ('that's why they call them plans') and his desperate 'ha ha' betraying his underlying feelings is a good character moment with comedic texture. The logic is comically circular and the laugh is clearly performative.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Hey, there you go.' — after helping Ross fill out 'just roommate' — then Ross: '"Thanks."' — with air quotes
jokes.setup: Joey has comforted Ross and helped fill in 'roommate' for the relationship field
jokes.punchline: Ross uses air quotes on 'thanks' — finally correctly deploying the air quotes concept, implying his thanks is insincere — which is funny as a callback to the entire air quotes subplot
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Ross uses air quotes correctly — after Joey's whole subplot of not knowing how to use them — and does so to deliver a sarcastic 'thanks' that also serves as emotional closure on their fight. It's a callback payoff, a character moment, AND a joke about their reconciliation all in one tiny gesture. The structure across the episode (Joey doesn't understand air quotes → Ross teaches him → Joey misuses them → Ross uses them perfectly at the end against Joey) is excellent long-form joke architecture. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Oh, my God. How long has she been crying?' Rachel: 'About a week and a half.'
jokes.setup: Joey returns to the apartment where Emma has been crying the whole time
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'about a week and a half' — obviously hyperbole but delivered flatly as if it's literally true
jokes.explanation: Classic exhausted-parent hyperbole delivered as fact. Good economy, gets the laugh from the flat delivery of an absurd duration.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Well, it looks like you guys got it under control, so I'm just gonna go.' — tries to leave immediately
jokes.setup: Joey has just walked into chaos — screaming baby, exhausted friends
jokes.punchline: He immediately attempts to escape with a transparently false 'you got it under control' — classic Joey self-preservation
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-preservation instinct is well-established; this is a reliable character beat. The obvious falseness of 'you got it under control' while Emma screams is a good ironic image.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'I'm the worst mother ever.' Monica: 'No, you're just new at this. Think about your first day at work. That couldn't have been easy, but you figured that out.' Rachel: 'Yeah, I don't think dressing provocatively is going to help me here!'
jokes.setup: Monica tries to reassure Rachel using a work analogy
jokes.punchline: Rachel's self-revelation that she dealt with her first work day by 'dressing provocatively' — immediately applying that logic to baby care and finding it unhelpful
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke. Monica's work analogy is meant to be comforting; Rachel's acceptance of it and then immediate application reveals something very true about her character — her main coping mechanism at work was appearance-based. The 'I don't think dressing provocatively is going to help me here' is both a confession and an application of logic that gets a big laugh. Strong Rachel character integration.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'I have to go to the bathroom.' Monica: 'Okay.' Rachel: 'I have to go scream into a pillow.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is at their wits' end with the crying baby; Monica takes Emma
jokes.punchline: Phoebe announces she needs the bathroom (normal) — Rachel escalates to needing to scream into a pillow (not normal), delivered with the same casual matter-of-fact tone as Phoebe's
jokes.explanation: Good parallel structure joke. Phoebe's mundane announcement sets up Rachel's escalated one, delivered in the exact same register. The deadpan equivalence between 'bathroom' and 'scream into a pillow' is the joke. Economy is very good.

jokes.text: Monica bouncing Emma: 'Have I gone deaf?'
jokes.setup: Monica has been bouncing Emma and the crying suddenly stops
jokes.punchline: Monica's first instinct is to wonder if she's gone deaf rather than believe the baby stopped crying
jokes.explanation: Four-word joke with tremendous economy. Monica's incredulity that the baby stopped crying — expressed as self-doubt about her own hearing rather than accepting the miracle — is a perfect new-parent joke. 'Have I gone deaf?' captures the exact experience of a sudden silence after hours of screaming.

jokes.text: Rachel, seeing Monica has calmed Emma: 'You must be a fireball in bed!'
jokes.setup: Monica has somehow bounced Emma to sleep when no one else could
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'you must be a fireball in bed' — connecting Monica's bouncing/soothing rhythm to sexual prowess in a totally unexpected direction
jokes.explanation: Genuinely unexpected direction for the joke — the logical leap from 'good at bouncing babies' to 'good in bed' is absurd but weirdly follows its own logic. It's a classic Rachel inappropriate-but-earnest compliment. Gets a solid laugh and is fairly quotable.

jokes.text: Monica: 'I have actual magical powers.'
jokes.setup: Monica has just gotten Emma to stop crying after everyone else failed
jokes.punchline: Monica's completely straight-faced attribution of her success to literal magic — no irony, total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Monica's competitive satisfaction at succeeding where others failed expressed as genuine magical ability. Very Monica in its confident self-aggrandizement. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Monica: 'I can hear traffic and birds. / I can hear the voices in my head again. / I'm kidding.'
jokes.setup: Monica is reveling in the sudden silence after the baby stopped crying
jokes.punchline: 'I can hear the voices in my head again' — escalating from normal sensory relief to implying she's been hearing voices, then immediately walking it back
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke — from traffic/birds (normal, relatable) to 'voices in my head' (alarming). The '...I'm kidding.' undercut is a good button, but the voice delivery would determine how well this lands. The dark-subversive element gives it more edge than typical Friends fare.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Yes, I did. I'm Monica, super aunt.'
jokes.setup: Rachel praises Monica for getting Emma to stop crying
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately brands herself with a superhero title: 'Monica, super aunt'
jokes.explanation: Functional Monica competitive-pride joke. The self-bestowed title is very Monica but the concept is familiar. Economy is solid.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'You're never leaving the apartment.' Monica: 'Say what?'
jokes.setup: Monica has just been declared 'official baby-crier stopper'
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately extends the honor into full-time servitude — 'you're never leaving the apartment' — Monica's 'Say what?' is perfect
jokes.explanation: Good quick exchange. Monica's 'Say what?' reaction is a fun character beat — she went from triumphant to trapped in two seconds. Light but functional.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Rachel? Let's give it six to eight months.'
jokes.setup: Monica is walking out on Rachel's attempts to press-gang her into permanent baby duty
jokes.punchline: 'Six to eight months' — the standard delivery timeline for a package, applied here to Monica's availability for Rachel's baby crisis
jokes.explanation: Good dry Monica burn. The shipping/delivery frame ('six to eight months') applied to her emotional availability is a fresh comedic construct. Gets a smile.

jokes.text: Chandler reveals they're moving to Tulsa to Monica in whispers because the baby is asleep. Monica screams 'WHAT?!' — everyone shushes — she tries to react in suppressed whisper-screams
jokes.setup: Chandler has to tell Monica they're moving to Tulsa but cannot make noise because Emma just fell asleep
jokes.punchline: Monica's explosive reaction to the news must be physically suppressed — the comedy is her trying to contain a full emotional breakdown to a whisper
jokes.explanation: One of the best scenes in the episode. The comedic concept — Monica receiving devastating news and being physically forced to suppress her reaction to protect the sleeping baby — is a brilliant structural device that creates layered comedy. Monica's character (explosive, intense, controlling) in direct conflict with the situation's requirement (absolute silence) is perfect. The whisper-screams, the shushing, the 'I can't... I can't hear' — this is a showcase physical comedy scene for Monica. The character integration is as high as it gets. Gets a 9 on impact because this is a sustained, escalating scene that builds and builds.

jokes.text: Ross arrives home with a cast/bandaged hand: 'If you think this is bad, you should see him. Ha ha.'
jokes.setup: Rachel asks what happened; Ross has his broken thumb
jokes.punchline: Ross's pride at coming off better in the altercation — 'you should see him' — which is ironic because Ross is the injured one; Joey is visually unharmed
jokes.explanation: Standard callback to the injury — 'you should see him' is a classic tough-guy joke delivered by someone who broke his own thumb punching a sign. The irony is implicit. Functional.

jokes.text: Rachel's 'big talk' about the Joey proposal resolves to: 'What I really, really want? I wanna sleep. I wanna eat. I wanna take a shower.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has built up a dramatic conversation about what she 'really, really wants' — the audience and Ross expect a romantic declaration
jokes.punchline: The deflation: she wants basic biological functions — sleep, food, shower
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection payoff. The dramatic build-up to Rachel's declaration — with Ross clearly hoping for a romantic resolution — punctured by 'I want to sleep, eat, and shower' is a solid comic deflation. It's also authentic new-mother comedy and works on both levels.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Emma: Not easy.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is summing up the experience of their first day home with the baby
jokes.punchline: The clipped, declarative 'Emma: Not easy.' — spoken like a product review or news headline
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy. Three words summing up the entire episode's A-plot. The declarative format — 'Emma: Not easy' — is funnier than any longer version would be. It lands as the thesis statement of the episode, delivered with perfect deadpan. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Joey returns to continue the argument with Ross: 'Uh, I've been thinking about this. I gotta tell you, it's not my fault. It's a natural instinct. / What would you do if I did this?' — presumably re-enacting the duck reflex
jokes.setup: Episode ends with Joey returning to relitigate the punching incident — specifically the duck reflex
jokes.punchline: Joey's re-demonstration of the head-fake/duck that caused the injury — presumably prompting Ross to duck again or react, closing on the same gag
jokes.explanation: Good tag-scene callback. Joey returning specifically to prove he was right about the reflex — when Ross has a broken thumb — is classic Joey logic. The physical comedy of the re-demonstration (inferred from the [23:10] gap suggesting visual business) closes the episode on a physical gag.

tmdb_overview: Chandler, having trouble getting enough sleep at home, falls asleep in a meeting and accidentally agrees to run his company's Tulsa office. Emma won't stop crying after Rachel interrupts her nap; Monica and Phoebe try to help get her back to sleep. Meanwhile, Ross is still mad at Joey, and breaks his finger trying to punch him.
insight: Post-birth comedy struggles: 66 score, 2.7 jokes/min signals Season 9 slump begins.
